title: Set-Jetting: Planning a Trip Around the Films and Shows You Love
metaDescription: Set-jetting is travel built around film and TV locations. The destinations driving it, how to visit responsibly, and how to plan a route that works.
excerpt: A single season of television can transform a town’s tourism overnight. Here is how to travel for the locations without wrecking them.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
Dubrovnik went from a beautiful, moderately visited Adriatic city to a place that had to install crowd counters at its gates. Parts of New Zealand built a permanent tourism identity around a film trilogy. A single Sicilian hotel became unbookable for a year after one season of television.

**Set-jetting** — travelling specifically to places you have seen on screen — is one of the strongest forces in modern tourism, and one of the least planned-for. Search interest in a location can multiply within days of a show airing, months before anyone in the destination has thought about how to handle it.

It is also, done thoughtfully, a genuinely good way to travel. A story gives you a reason to go somewhere you would never have picked from a map.

## Why It Works as a Trip Structure

A film or series gives you three things a guidebook does not.

**A route.** Productions shoot in clusters, which means the locations of a single season often form a coherent regional itinerary — one you would have struggled to assemble yourself.

**A reason to go somewhere unfashionable.** Some of the best set-jetting destinations are places with no independent tourism pull. A show sends you to a region you would otherwise have driven past.

**Emotional weight.** Standing somewhere you have watched dozens of times is a specific and surprisingly strong feeling. It is the same instinct that makes literary pilgrimage work.

![Travel Trends travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1505832018823-50331d70d237?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## The Destinations Driving It

**Croatia — Dubrovnik and Šibenik.** The best-known example, and a cautionary tale. Dubrovnik's old town is small, and the volume of visitors it now receives forced the city into active crowd management. Go, but go early in the morning or in shoulder season, and give Šibenik and Trogir the time they deserve.

**New Zealand.** The most mature set-jetting economy on earth. Fully developed tour infrastructure across both islands, and the landscapes justify the trip entirely on their own merits.

**Sicily and the Amalfi Coast.** Recent prestige television has driven enormous interest in Taormina, Noto and the Aeolian Islands. Prices at the specific hotels featured have risen accordingly; the surrounding towns have not, which is where the value is.

**Scotland and Northumberland.** Castles, coastline and moorland that have served a very long list of productions. Doubles as one of the best road trips in Britain.

**Iceland.** Used repeatedly as an alien or ancient landscape. Most of the well-known filming locations sit along accessible routes rather than in the remote interior.

**Northern Ireland.** Compact, dramatic and heavily filmed, with the Causeway Coast as the spine of any route.

**Spain — Seville, Girona, the Basque coast.** Frequently standing in for other places entirely, which is part of the fun.

**Japan and South Korea.** A large and growing category driven by anime, film and K-drama, with fan pilgrimage to specific neighbourhoods, cafés and stations. Here especially, the etiquette section below matters.

**India — Rajasthan, Kashmir, Ladakh.** Decades of Bollywood locations, many of them spectacular and most of them still primarily visited by domestic travellers.

![Travel Trends travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1551801691-f0bce83d4f68?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## How to Plan a Set-Jetting Route

**Find the real locations, not the fictional ones.** A single fictional place is routinely assembled from four locations in three countries. Production location lists and regional film commission websites are far more reliable than fan maps.

**Cluster geographically, not narratively.** Visiting locations in story order will send you back and forth across a country. Group them by region and accept that you are seeing episode nine before episode two.

**Check access before you commit.** Many locations are private property, working farms, active religious sites or homes. Some are accessible only on an official tour. Some are not accessible at all, and turning up anyway is trespassing.

**Book the famous ones early.** If a specific hotel, restaurant or room featured on screen, assume it is booked months ahead and priced accordingly.

**Build in the non-screen stuff.** The mistake is treating the trip as a checklist of frames to reproduce. The regions are usually wonderful independently; leave room for that.

## Visiting Responsibly

Set-jetting has caused real harm in specific places, and it is worth being clear about why.

The problem is **concentration**. Normal tourism spreads across a season and a region. Set-jetting funnels a large number of people to one street, one staircase, one café, often within a few months of a release, in destinations with no capacity to absorb it. Some towns have installed barriers, restricted access or actively asked visitors to stop coming.

Practical etiquette:

- **Residential streets are people's homes.** If a location is a doorway on a residential street, photograph it quickly and quietly, and do not gather.
- **Go outside peak hours.** Early morning transforms the experience for you and reduces the load on the location.
- **Spend money locally.** The strongest argument for this kind of tourism is that it supports the place. Eat, stay and shop in the town rather than arriving by coach and leaving after twenty minutes.
- **Respect signs and closures.** When a site says no access, that is usually because too many people ignored a politer version of the same request.
- **Do not recreate scenes that involve climbing on things.** A depressing amount of location damage is people getting into position for a photograph.

## A Better Way to Frame the Trip

The most rewarding set-jetting trips treat the screen locations as an **excuse and a spine**, not the whole body. You go to Northern Ireland for the coastline you saw in a title sequence and stay for the coast road, the seafood and the small towns nobody filmed.

Plan it as a regional road trip with a handful of locations anchoring the route, and let the rest be ordinary travel. That produces both a better holiday and a lighter footprint on the places that did not ask to become famous.

If you are planning it with friends — and set-jetting is a natural group trip, because the shared reference is the whole point — map the locations against the driving route before you commit to anything. Two locations that look adjacent on a fan map are frequently three hours apart. Laying the route out properly in **Trypinn** first will save you a day of driving you did not plan for.
